blocks.text: Antoninus Liberalis, Fab. 28, from Nicander: Ἀπόλλων μὲν ἐγένετο ἱέραξ, Ἑρμῆς δὲ ἴβις, Ἄρης δὲ λεπιδωτὸς ἰχθὺς, Ἄρτεμις δὲ αἴλουρος [Apollōn men egeneto hierax, Hermēs de ibis, Arēs de lepidōtos ichthys, Artemis de ailouros] (so it must be read instead of σίλουρος [silouros], as is clear from Ovid) τράγῳ δὲ εἰκάζεται Διόνυσος, ἔλλῳ δὲ Ἡρακλῆς, βοὶ δ᾽ Ἥφαιστος, μυγάλῃ δὲ Λητώ [tragō de eikazetai Dionysos, ellō de Hēraklēs, boi d' Hēphaistos, mygalē de Lētō]: Apollo was changed into a hawk, Mercury into an ibis, Mars into a scaly fish, Diana into a cat, Bacchus into a goat, Hercules into a fawn, Vulcan into an ox, Latona into a shrew-mouse. We do not undertake to explain all of these here, but only a few, for whose invention the occasion was taken from paronomasias. Jupiter, the supreme God, was changed into a ram, because אל el, God the strong, and איל ajil, ram, are paronyms, and the plural of both is אלים elim. Bacchus, the Osiris of the Egyptians, into a he-goat, because שעיר seir, in Hebrew he-goat, alludes to Osiris. Diana into a cat, because in Egyptian ΒΟΥΒΑΣΤΟΣ was the cat, and Bubastis was Diana. The one is in Stephanus, under the word Βούβαστος [Boubastos]: Οἱ δὲ Αἰγύπτιοι βούβαστον τὴν αἴλουρόν φασι [Hoi de Aigyptioi boubaston tēn ailouron phasi]: but the Egyptians call the cat bubastos; the other in Herodotus, book 2, ch. 156: Αἰγυπτιστὶ δὲ Ἀπόλλων Ὧρος, Δημήτηρ δὲ Ἶσις, Ἄρτεμις δὲ Βούβαστις [Aigyptisti de Apollōn Hōros, Dēmētēr de Isis, Artemis de Boubastis]: in Egyptian Apollo is Horus, Ceres Isis, Diana Bubastis. Hence it is that in the Herbarium of Apuleius, ch. 10, the Egyptians call Artemisia Βουβαστέως καρδίαν [Boubasteōs kardian], the heart of Bubastis, that is, the herb dear to Diana, as its Greek name also displays. Juno took the shape of a cow. For we have observed in its place that עשתרות, from which Juno was called Astarte, signifies not only flocks of sheep but also herds of cattle, and that this is why in Sanchuniathon Astarte ἐπέθηκε τῇ ἰδίᾳ κεφαλῇ βασιλείας παράσημον κεφαλὴν ταύρου [epethēke tē idia kephalē basileias parasēmon kephalēn taurou], placed a bull's head on her own head as the insignia of royalty. That Venus hid in a fish they refer to Atargatis, as if she were Dagon, to whom דג dag, that is, fish, gave the name; but I approve this less, for reasons given elsewhere.

[II, 607] Hezekiah in his illness says that he chirped like a swallow [Ies. XXXVIII, 14.], because the swallow's voice seems to have something plaintive and mournful about it. All the poets proclaim this with one voice. Hesiod, in the Works, verse 366:
Τὸν δὲ μετ' ὀρθρογόη Πανδιονὶς ὦρτο χελιδὼν, [Ton de met' orthrogoē Pandionis ōrto chelidōn,]

After him, lamenting at dawn, came forth the swallow, daughter of Pandion. Hence Suidas: Ὀρθρογόη· χελιδών [Orthrogoē: chelidōn]. Others prefer ὀρθογόη [orthogoē]. Hesychius: Ὀρθογόη· ἡ χελιδών [Orthogoē: hē chelidōn]. Accordingly, from this, Ὀρθογόν· χελιδών [Orthogon: chelidōn] must be corrected in the manuscript Lexicon of Cyril in my possession. In the Etymologicum ὀρθογόη [orthogoē] is rendered ἡ μεγάλως θρηνοῦσα [hē megalōs thrēnousa], she who laments greatly. So too in Phavorinus, who adds that it is said of the swallow. Aristophanes in the Frogs:

Δὴ χείλεσιν ἀμφιλάλοις Δεινὸν ἐπιβρέμεται Θρηΐκια χελιδὼν, Ἐπὶ βάρβαρον ἑζομένη πέταλον, Κελαδεῖ δ' ἐπίκλαυτον ἀηδόνιον νόμον, [Dē cheilesin amphilalois Deinon epibremetai Thrēikia chelidōn, Epi barbaron hezomenē petalon, Keladei d' epiklauton aēdonion nomon,]
Now with chattering lips the Thracian swallow resounds heavily, sitting upon a barbarian leaf, and sings a mournful, shrill song.
Moschus, Idyll 3:
Οὐδὲ τόσον θρήνησεν ἀν' ὤρεα μακρὰ χελιδὼν, [Oude toson thrēnēsen an' ōrea makra chelidōn,]
Nor did the swallow lament so much across the great mountains. Palladas, Anthol. book 1, ch. 60:
Τίπτε πανημέριος, Πανδιονὶ κάμμορε κούρη, [col. 64] Μυρομένη κελαδεῖς τραυλὰ διὰ στομάτων. [Tipte panēmerios, Pandioni kammore kourē, Myromenē keladeis traula dia stomatōn.]
Why all day long, O daughter of Pandion, unhappy girl, do you sing lamenting, lisping songs from your mouth? Accordingly, on these lines of Theocritus in the Thalysia,
— — — — ἁ δ' ἐλολυγὼν Τηλόθεν ἐν πυκινῇσι βάτων τρύζεσκεν ἀκάνθαις, [ha d' elolygōn Tēlothen en pykinēsi batōn tryzesken akanthais,]

And the ololygon moaned far off in the dense thorns of the brambles, ὀλολυγὼν [ololygōn] is explained by the Scholiast as ἡ χελιδὼν ἡ τὸν Ἴτυν ὀλοφυρομένη [hē chelidōn hē ton Ityn olophyromenē], the swallow bewailing Itys. And Agathias, Anthol. book 7, Epigr. 65, addresses the swallows thus:
Ἀλλ' Ἴτυλον κλαίοιτε κατ' οὔρεα, καὶ γοάοιτε, [All' Itylon klaioite kat' ourea, kai goaoite,]

But bewail Itylus in the mountains, and lament. Nor do the Roman poets speak otherwise. Catullus to Ortalus: [II, 608] Such as beneath the dense shade of the branches the Daulian bird sings, moaning the fate of the lost Itylus.
Horace, book 4, Ode 12:
The unhappy bird builds her nest, tearfully moaning Itys, etc. — — —
C. Albinovanus to Livia:
The Daulian bird bewails Thracian Itys.
Ovid, Tristia book 5, Eleg. 1:
It is something to relieve a fatal ill by words; this makes Procne and the halcyons plaintive.
Seneca in Hercules Oetaeus, Act 1:
— — — as the Daulian bird is wont to weep for her son beneath the Ismarian shade. — —
And in Agamemnon, Act 3:
Not the Bistonian bird that sits on the rooftops, chattering bewails the impious thefts of her dread husband.
And in Hercules Furens, Act 1:
And the Thracian concubine longs to give her wings to the new sun among her plaintive nests. — —
